docs.title: Welcome to the Innovation Workshop
docs.text:
The CNSI Innovation Workshop includes the rapid prototyping facility in Elings 3430 and the Machining Hub in Elings 2442.

These are shared recharge facilities that have a wide selection of 3D printers (resin and FDM), polymer casting equipment, a 100W laser cutter, and a variety of both CNC and manual machine tools.

Dr. Brian Dincau and the Innovation Workshop staff (Workshop Wizards) can teach you how to use any of our equipment and, perhaps more importantly, help you figure out how to quickly turn an idea into a functional prototype or experiment. We have experience spanning biology, engineering, physics, marine science, art, architecture, and more. See our Projects page for a far-from-comprehensive overview of some of our past collaborations.

The Innovation Workshop is open to all UCSB research groups, student clubs, and industry users.

docs.title: Our History
docs.text:
The Innovation Workshop has its roots in a much larger story at UC Santa Barbara: the development of Elings Hall and the California NanoSystems Institute (CNSI) as a place where researchers from across the university could share specialized tools, facilities, and expertise.

What began as an effort to make microfluidics fabrication more accessible eventually grew into a broad fabrication and rapid-prototyping resource serving researchers, students, entrepreneurs, and the wider UCSB community.

The names and rooms have changed over the years, but the underlying mission has remained remarkably consistent:

Give people access to the tools, expertise, and workspace they need to turn an idea into something real.

docs.title: From CNSI to Elings Hall
docs.text:
How Elings Hall and CNSI established the foundation for shared research facilities

The story begins with the creation of the California Institutes for Science and Innovation in 2000, which included the California NanoSystems Institute at UC Santa Barbara and UCLA.

Construction of the CNSI building at UCSB began following a 2003 groundbreaking. The planned $53 million, 110,904-square-foot building was designed around interdisciplinary research, with modular laboratories and shared facilities including a state-of-the-art cleanroom, imaging and spectroscopy facilities, bio-nanofabrication laboratories, and computational resources.

UCSB: UC Santa Barbara Breaks Ground on Building to House Pioneering California NanoSystems Institute

The building was subsequently named Elings Hall following a $12.5 million gift from Virgil Elings and Betty Elings Wells in 2007. The gift provided substantial support for CNSI research and helped establish the building as a long-term home for interdisciplinary science and technology at UCSB.

UCSB: UCSB Receives $12.5 Million Gift from Virgil Elings and Betty Elings Wells

From the beginning, Elings Hall was intended to be more than a collection of conventional laboratories. Its shared facilities were designed to give researchers access to sophisticated equipment and expertise that would be difficult for individual research groups to maintain on their own.

That philosophy would eventually lead to the creation of the Microfluidics Lab and, later, the Innovation Workshop.

docs.title: The Microfluidics Lab
docs.text:
From cleanroom bottleneck to accessible fabrication

Before the Microfluidics Lab existed, UCSB researchers working with microfluidic devices often relied on the campus cleanroom and the semiconductor and MEMS fabrication infrastructure that had developed around it.

UCSB had a long history of semiconductor manufacturing, and during the late 1990s and early 2000s, that work expanded into microelectromechanical systems (MEMS). These devices could be fabricated using many of the same techniques and equipment developed for semiconductor manufacturing.

As microfluidics became increasingly important across many areas of research, however, the cleanroom presented a significant barrier to experimentation.

The cleanroom was extraordinarily capable, but it was not an easy environment for someone to enter simply to try an idea. There were startup costs, extensive training requirements, and restrictions on who could use the facility. According to longtime CNSI development engineer Dave Bothman, it could take approximately six months to learn to use the cleanroom tools safely, and undergraduates were not permitted to use the facility.

Most microfluidics research, however, did not require a cleanroom for every step of the process.

This created a bottleneck. Researchers who needed microfluidic devices but did not have direct access to the cleanroom sometimes relied on an informal, word-of-mouth system in which someone else would fabricate the device for them.

It worked, but it was not particularly fast.

Recognizing this problem, Bothman suggested to CNSI administrators that UCSB establish a dedicated microfluidics laboratory in Elings Hall.

UCSB Mechanical Engineering: The Microfluidics Lab — Enabler of Experimentation

docs.title: Establishing the Microfluidics Lab
docs.text:
Around 2012, the Microfluidics Lab was established in Elings 3430.

The lab was deliberately conceived as an enabling facility. Rather than conducting a particular line of research of its own, the MFL provided researchers with the equipment and expertise needed to fabricate the physical devices required for their experiments.

This was a significant change in the way microfluidic fabrication could be approached at UCSB.

Instead of:

I need access to a cleanroom before I can even begin experimenting...

researchers could increasingly approach the Microfluidics Lab with:

I have an idea. How can we make it?

By 2013, the Microfluidics Lab was already operating as a substantial shared facility. Its equipment included tools and processes for PDMS mixing and casting, spin coating, ozone treatment, wafer bonding, microscopy, CNC cutting and drilling, and other forms of microfluidic fabrication.

The Microfluidics Lab became an important bridge between UCSB's highly specialized nanofabrication infrastructure and the researchers who simply needed to make something and test an idea.

That idea — make sophisticated fabrication accessible to more people — would become the foundation of the Innovation Workshop.

docs.title: The Innovation Workshop Emerges
docs.text:
How the Innovation Workshop grew alongside the Microfluidics Lab

The Innovation Workshop grew out of the same need for accessible, shared fabrication resources.

By 2016, CNSI documentation was already identifying the Microfluidics Lab and Innovation Workshop together as shared facilities, with Dave Bothman overseeing both.

The two facilities had complementary purposes.

The Microfluidics Lab, located in Elings 3430, focused on microfluidic fabrication and related laboratory processes. The Innovation Workshop, located in Elings 2442 and 2448, provided a more general-purpose environment for rapid prototyping and fabrication.

By this point, the Workshop was moving beyond the specialized world of microfluidics. Its purpose was broader: provide researchers, students, and emerging companies with a place where they could rapidly build, modify, and test physical ideas.

Historical documentation from the period shows the Innovation Workshop containing mechanical and electronic assembly tools, a CNC router, bandsaw, drill press, laser cutter, 3D scanner, and 3D printers, while the Microfluidics Lab contained both specialized microfluidic equipment and additional fabrication tools.

The two spaces were therefore not competing facilities. They were two expressions of the same philosophy:

Make fabrication accessible.

docs.title: The 2018 Expansion
docs.text:
A major expansion brought new rapid-prototyping and additive manufacturing capabilities

A major expansion came through California Assembly Bill 2664, which provided $22 million across the University of California system to expand innovation and entrepreneurship infrastructure.

At UCSB, the resulting investment helped expand the campus's innovation ecosystem and provided funding for a substantially expanded Innovation Workshop.

UCSB: Innovation and Entrepreneurship Expansion

The expanded Workshop brought together capabilities including 3D printing, laser cutting, CNC routing, electronics assembly, programming, and traditional hand tools.

By 2019, the Workshop included seven high-end 3D printers, along with laser-cutting, CNC, electronics, and general prototyping capabilities.

UCSB Electrical & Computer Engineering: Convergence, Spring 2019

The result was a powerful combination:

  • Microfluidics Lab: specialized fabrication for microfluidic devices and scientific research
  • Innovation Workshop: rapid prototyping, mechanical fabrication, electronics, and general-purpose making

Together, the spaces gave researchers a way to move much more quickly from an idea to a physical prototype.

docs.title: COVID-19 and the Workshop Wizards
docs.text:
How the pandemic changed the Innovation Workshop and helped shape the Workshop Wizards

The role of the Workshop changed again during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Before the pandemic, the shared facilities served approximately 300 users from 90 research groups and CNSI incubator companies.

When access to campus laboratories was restricted in 2020, CNSI staff adapted the Workshop so that users could submit designs and have parts fabricated for them rather than needing to enter the facility themselves.

When PPE was in short supply due to global supply chain issues, we utilized our 3D printers to make lightweight face shields for the campus.

UCSB: Printing Protection

This experience helped establish a new model for the Workshop: users did not always need to operate the machines themselves. They could bring a problem or design to the Workshop, and the staff and student workers could help turn it into a physical object.

docs.title: The Workshop Wizards
docs.text:
This eventually led to the development of the Workshop Wizards, an undergraduate program in which students learn to operate and maintain the Workshop's equipment while helping fabricate parts and devices for researchers.

The Wizards maintain equipment, provide training, design new tools, and build parts for users.

The program transformed the Workshop into more than a collection of machines. It became a place where students could learn practical fabrication, machining, electronics, design, and problem-solving by working on real research and engineering projects.

UCSB Mechanical Engineering: Young Wizards at the Microfluidics Lab

docs.title: From Microfluidics to Rhinoceros Stents
docs.text:
An unusual project demonstrates the power of rapid prototyping

One of the clearest examples of what the combined facilities could accomplish came from an unusual collaboration involving a black rhinoceros named Layla.

CNSI collaborated with the Chicago Brookfield Zoo to develop a custom sinus stent for Layla. Between 2020 and 2022, the Workshop Wizards helped fabricate 14 iterations of the design, with some iterations being produced in as little as one to two days.

CNSI: CNSI and Layla the Rhinoceros

The project demonstrated something fundamental about the Workshop.

The value of a shared fabrication facility is not simply the machines themselves. It is the ability to move rapidly through a cycle of:

Design → Fabrication → Testing → Redesign → Fabrication

That cycle is at the heart of modern rapid prototyping.

docs.title: 2024: A New Chapter
docs.text:
The Microfluidics Lab and Innovation Workshop become one fabrication ecosystem

In the summer of 2024, Elings 2448 was converted into an Incubator Lab.

This change reduced the Workshop's available footprint by approximately 30%.

Rather than simply trying to fit the old organization into a smaller space, we took the opportunity to reconsider what the Workshop actually was.

The answer was clear:

The Microfluidics Lab and the Innovation Workshop had become one fabrication ecosystem.

The name Microfluidics Lab described how the facility began, but it no longer described the full range of work taking place there.

So we reorganized the facilities around their current capabilities rather than their historical names.

docs.title: Future Makers: Bringing Making to the Next Generation
docs.text:
Extending the Workshop's mission to local K–12 students

The Innovation Workshop's mission to make fabrication accessible does not stop at UCSB's research community. In 2025, that mission expanded beyond the university through the creation of the Future Makers Program, a partnership between the CNSI Innovation Workshop and Los Ingenieros, a UCSB student organization dedicated to mentoring and inspiring future Latin@ STEM graduates.

Future Makers was created around a simple idea: many children never get the opportunity to use the kinds of tools that makers and engineers take for granted.

3D printers, laser cutters, CNC machines, electronics, and even basic fabrication tools can seem completely inaccessible to a young student. But giving a child the opportunity to make something with those tools can change how they see themselves — not just as a student, but as someone capable of designing and building things.

The program received an Uplift Central Coast Catalyst Predevelopment Grant in February 2025. Future Makers was one of 36 projects selected from 136 applicants competing for a share of a $9 million grant program.

CNSI: Innovation Workshop Supports "Future Makers" with Uplift Central Coast Catalyst Predevelopment Grant

docs.title: From Grant to Reality
docs.text:
The first Future Makers field trip took place in late 2025, when fourth- through sixth-grade students from Glen City Elementary in Santa Paula visited Elings Hall.

The students spent the day exploring UCSB before coming to the Innovation Workshop, where they used 3D printers, a laser cutter, and a robotic sticker cutter to create personalized trading cards based on their interests, favorite subjects, animals, and dreams.

The activity was developed and led by Innovation Workshop Manager Brian Dincau and the Workshop Wizards, who spent months refining the project to make sure it was safe, engaging, and accessible for elementary-school students.

UCSB: UCSB Program Broadens STEM Opportunity for Underserved Youth

The response from the students demonstrated exactly what the program was designed to accomplish.

Rather than simply teaching students how to operate a machine, Future Makers gives them the experience of making something that belongs to them. The students make decisions, experiment with unfamiliar technology, and leave campus holding something they designed themselves.

That distinction is important.

The goal is not simply to introduce children to STEM careers. It is to help them see themselves as people who can participate in those careers.

The first visit was only the beginning. The Uplift Central Coast grant supported nine Future Makers field trips, bringing students from Lompoc, Santa Maria, and Santa Paula to UCSB.

Future Makers represents a natural extension of the Innovation Workshop's history.

The Microfluidics Lab was originally created to make advanced fabrication accessible to researchers who could not easily use the cleanroom.

The Innovation Workshop expanded that philosophy to students, entrepreneurs, and anyone with an idea they wanted to prototype.

The Workshop Wizards turned that philosophy into a hands-on learning experience for UCSB undergraduates.

And Future Makers carries it one step further — bringing the opportunity to make, experiment, and imagine directly to students who may never have had access to these tools before.

You don't have to know what you want to build before you walk through the door. Sometimes you just need someone to show you that you can build something at all.

docs.title: Elings 3430 — Innovation Workshop
docs.text:
Elings 3430 is now the Innovation Workshop proper.

The name Microfluidics Lab has been retired, but its capabilities have not disappeared.

The equipment and processes that made the original Microfluidics Lab valuable remain in 3430. Users can still fabricate microfluidic devices and work with the specialized equipment developed over years of microfluidics research and experimentation.

At the same time, 3D printing has been consolidated into 3430, bringing additive manufacturing together with the Workshop's other rapid-prototyping and fabrication capabilities.

Today, the Innovation Workshop in 3430 includes a mixture of:

  • 3D printers
  • Microfluidics and PDMS-processing equipment
  • Laser cutting
  • Polymer fabrication
  • Specialized CNC equipment
  • Electronics and general prototyping tools
  • Microscopy and inspection equipment
  • Other specialized fabrication equipment

The result is a space where a user can move between very different fabrication techniques without needing to decide whether their project belongs to a "microfluidics lab" or a "makerspace."

The current CNSI description reflects this broader role, describing the Innovation Workshop as a rapid-prototyping facility equipped for polymer casting, laser cutting, additive manufacturing, and more.

CNSI: Innovation Workshop

docs.title: Innovation Workshop Machine Hub
docs.text:
The former Workshop space has also evolved.

Elings 2442 is now the Innovation Workshop Machine Hub.

The Machine Hub is intentionally focused on a different class of fabrication than the main Workshop.

Its emphasis is on:

  • Manual machine tools
  • Hand tools
  • Traditional mechanical fabrication
  • General machining
  • Waterjet cutting

The Machine Hub includes a suite of traditional machining tools as well as a waterjet cutter capable of processing a wide range of materials.

CNSI: Machining Hub

docs.title: Access & Training
docs.text:
The UCSB Innovation Workshop is a shared fabrication facility available to researchers at the University of California, Santa Barbara. The Workshop also accommodates student project teams, including Capstone, New Ventures, and Bren EcoE programs, as well as approved users from outside UCSB.

Access to the Innovation Workshop requires completion of the following steps in order:

  1. Facility Access Request
  2. New User Orientation
  3. UC Laboratory Safety Training
  4. Card-Key Access

docs.title: Who Can Use the Innovation Workshop?
docs.text:
The Innovation Workshop is available to: - UCSB undergraduates, graduate students, post docs, professors, and other university staff working on UC-funded projects - Companies that want to use the Innovation Workshop for prototyping or testing new equipment - Elementary, middle school, and high school groups for tours and maker activities

If you are unsure if the Innovation Workshop is the right place for your work, contact the lab manager Brian Dincau (bdincau@ucsb.edu)

docs.title: Getting Access to the Innovation Workshop
docs.text: New users must complete the following four steps before receiving card-key access to the Workshop.

docs.title: 1. Facility Access Request
docs.text:
Before using any CNSI shared facility, you must submit the initial Facility Access Request through the CNSI.

Submit the Facility Access Request

docs.title: CCOA Accounting String
docs.text:
Academic users must have their CCOA accounting string available when completing the Facility Access Request.

Your CCOA accounting string must be verified before you can proceed with Workshop training.

docs.title: 2. New User Orientation
docs.text:
All new users must complete the Innovation Workshop New User Orientation before receiving card-key access to the Workshop.

The orientation introduces users to the Workshop's facilities, general safety requirements, access procedures, and expectations for working in the labs.

After submitting your Facility Access Request, use the Training Request Form to request:

  • New User Orientation
  • Training on specific Workshop tools

Request New User Orientation or Tool Training

Important: Submit your Facility Access Request before requesting New User Orientation or tool training.

docs.title: 3. UC Laboratory Safety Training
docs.text:
The University of California requires everyone working in a laboratory to complete the online UC Laboratory Safety Fundamentals training.

The initial training must be completed before card-key access can be approved. A refresher is required annually.

docs.title: How to Complete the Training
docs.text:
1. Go to the UCSB Learning Center and log in.
  2. Search for Fundamentals of Laboratory Safety.
  3. Complete the online course.
  4. If you have already completed the initial course, complete the required annual refresher if prompted.
  5. Send a copy of your completion certificate to the Workshop Manager.

docs.title: Undergraduate Users
docs.text: If you are an undergraduate and cannot log in to the UCSB Learning Center, contact your PI or advisor. They can request that the system send you an invitation to enroll in the required training.

docs.title: 4. Card-Key Access
docs.text:
After completing the Facility Access Request, New User Orientation, and required Laboratory Safety Training, you can request card-key access to the Innovation Workshop.

The card-key access form is only available when connected to the UCSB campus network or VPN.

Request Card-Key Access

docs.title: Workshop Rooms
docs.text:
The Innovation Workshop occupies two rooms in Elings Hall:

  • Elings 3430
  • Elings 2442

When requesting access, be sure to request access to both Workshop rooms as well as the appropriate exterior doors.

Tip: If you want your Workshop access approved as quickly as possible, request only the Workshop rooms and exterior doors. Submit a separate card-key request for access to other CNSI rooms.

docs.title: Lab Safety
docs.text: Here you can find our Chemical Inventory as well as general safety information for the Innovation Workshop and Machine Hub.

docs.title: Personal Protection Equipment
docs.text:
Long pants and closed-toed shoes are required at ALL times in both labs to protect oneself from physical hazards, such as sharp or heavy objects.

Safety Glasses, Face Shields, Work Gloves, Earplugs, Earmuffs, Nitrile Gloves, and Dust Masks are available as needed.

If you need a Lab Coat for you work, you must bring your own.

docs.title: Other Safety Considerations
docs.text:
First Aid Kits with band aids and antiseptic are available in both labs. In 3440, they are located on the consumables rack. In 2442, they are located on top of the blue tool chest.

Fire Extinguishers are available by the front door for each lab. A Halon extinguisher and fire blanket are co-located by the laser cutter in 3430.

docs.title: Safety Concerns
docs.text:
Serious injury and potential dismemberment can occur from contact with the moving saw blade.

Eye injuries can result from flying chips or broken bits. Cuts can occur from contacting sharp tools or exposed chips and burrs. Burns can result from hot cutting tools or parts. Metal splinters can result from exposed burrs or chips. Serious injury can result from pinching or entanglement in moving parts.

Poor housekeeping creates tripping and cutting hazards for other users. Do not leave the machine running unattended.

Eye protection, closed-toe shoes, long pants, and protective clothing must be worn when using this machine to prevent injury. Long hair must be tied back and jewelry must be removed before operating this machine to prevent entanglement.

docs.title: Training Requirements
docs.text:
Before using this machine, users must:

  • Take and pass the Machine Shop Safety test found on the ME Labs GauchoSpace page.
  • Read the Drill Press document on the Innovation Workshop GauchoSpace page.
  • Attend Innovation Workshop general machine-tool training.
  • Complete Innovation Workshop bandsaw-specific training.
  • Review additional documents found on the GauchoSpace page.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Materials: Ferrous metals, non-ferrous metals, wood, and plastic can be cut on this saw. If you have questions about a new material, email the material in question to ‪bdincau@ucsb.edu.
  • Blade: Keep fingers at least 3 inches away from the saw blade at all times. Lower the blade cover to 1/4 inch above the workpiece to minimize the risk of injury.
  • Exhaust: Use the exhaust system to prevent inhalation of dust and particulates. Use brushes and the shop vacuum to clean up residual chips and dust.
  • Emergency: Call 911 or 9-911 from a campus phone if serious injury occurs. First-aid supplies are located near the sink in 2448 Elings.

docs.title: Physical Safety
docs.text:
• The saw blade can cause serious injury and dismemberment.
  • Keep fingers at least 3 inches away from the saw blade at all times.
  • Keep the saw blade cover no more than 1/4 inch above the surface of the stock to minimize blade exposure.
  • Exercise caution when cutting large stock. Ensure there is ample clearance around the machine.
  • Keep the work area clean. A cluttered work area presents multiple hazards.
  • The machine is kept locked until the online reservation system can be implemented. Lab staff will keep it unlocked during the workday and can unlock it upon request if needed.
  • Use the exhaust system and shop vacuum to prevent inhalation of particulates.

docs.title: Sequence of Operation
docs.text:
1. Move the saw out from the alcove if cutting large stock.
  2. Adjust the rip fence to the proper length for the cut. Lock the rip fence in place.
  3. Adjust the saw blade cover to 1/4 inch above the workpiece. Tighten the blade cover in place.
  4. Power on the motor controller. The power switch is located on the side of the unit.
  5. Select the proper material setting on the motor controller. Press once to select the material group, then press the button to cycle through to the appropriate material setting.
  6. Press On to start the bandsaw.
  7. Turn the exhaust system on.
  8. Hold the material securely while keeping fingers at least 3 inches away from the saw blade. Use the push stick if necessary.
  9. Push the material through the saw blade evenly and slowly. If the saw blade chatters or screams, ease off the feed pressure.
  10. Once the cut is complete, press Off on the motor controller to stop the bandsaw. Do not reach for the parts at this time. Turn the exhaust system off as well.
  11. Once the saw blade has come to a complete stop, remove your parts. Use a brush or shop vacuum to clean up any remaining dust and chips.
  12. Extend the saw blade cover to cover the entire blade.
  13. Power off the motor controller. The motor controller stays illuminated for approximately 15 seconds after switching the power off.
  14. Return the bandsaw to the alcove.
  15. Clean up any remaining dust and debris from the floor.

docs.title: Supplies
docs.text:
• Bandsaw blades are kept in the cabinet of the bandsaw stand. Notify lab staff by emailing ‪bdincau@ucsb.edu if you break a bandsaw blade. Lab staff will replace it.
  • The resaw bar assembly is kept in the cabinet of the bandsaw stand. Use the resaw bar assembly to prevent the bandsaw blade from walking or moving during the cut.

docs.title: Recommended Blade Selection and Speed
docs.text:
In general, at least three cutting teeth should be in contact with the material being cut at all times. Thinner materials therefore require a finer-tooth blade than thicker materials.

Please see lab staff for instruction on changing bandsaw blades.

The bandsaw motor connects to the blade drive through a two-speed belt drive. The belt must be in the low range when cutting stainless steel and titanium. All other materials may be cut with the belt in the high range.

The controller has four pre-programmed material categories:

  • Wood
  • Metal
  • Non-ferrous metals
  • Plastic

Within each category, four material types are programmed. Preset speeds are listed in two units: surface feet per minute (SFPM) and revolutions per minute (RPM).

The conversion factor between SFPM and RPM changes depending on the position of the belt on the drive pulley.

The speed-adjustment dial on the controller can be used to increase or decrease the speed from the preset levels. If the saw is making excessive noise, try lowering the speed.

docs.title: Bandsaw Feeds and Speeds
docs.text:
General rule of thumb for TPI: Always have a minimum of 3 teeth engaged in the material at any given time.

docs.title: CNSI Drill Press SOP
docs.text: Revised: August 2020 Compiled with help from the UCSB ME Design Lab SOP written by Dr. Trevor Marks.

docs.title: Location
docs.text: The WEN 15-inch floor-standing drill press is located in Elings Hall 2448.

docs.title: Safety Concerns
docs.text:
Eye injuries can result from flying chips or broken bits. Sharp tools, chips, and burrs can cause cuts or metal splinters. Cutting tools and parts may cause burns. Moving parts can pinch or entangle clothing, hair, or jewelry. Poor housekeeping creates tripping and cutting hazards for other users. Do not leave the machine running unattended.

Wear eye protection, closed-toe shoes, long pants, and protective clothing when using this machine. Tie back long hair and remove jewelry before operating the machine to prevent entanglement.

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
Before using this machine:

  1. Take and pass the Machine Shop Safety test on the ME Labs GauchoSpace page.
  2. Read the Drill Press document on the Innovation Workshop GauchoSpace page.
  3. Attend the Innovation Workshop general machine tool training.
  4. Attend the Innovation Workshop drill press-specific training.

Additional documents are available on the GauchoSpace page.

docs.title: Safe Materials to Drill
docs.text:
• Aluminum: Use lubricant (WD-40).
  • Brass: Use lubricant.
  • Plastic: Do not use lubricant.
  • Wood: Do not use lubricant.

docs.title: Before Drilling
docs.text:
1. Check that you are complying with all PPE guidelines.
  2. Lay out and center-punch the holes you wish to drill.
  3. Collect the tools needed for the operation. Inspect them to ensure they are sharp and in good condition. Do not use end mills or Dremel bits in the drill press.
  4. Insert the bit into the drill chuck, tighten it with the chuck key, and remove the chuck key before continuing. Do not tighten the chuck by powering on the machine or leave the chuck key in the chuck. Both are extremely dangerous practices.
  5. Align the holes with the drill bit and secure the part using the vise or drill bed clamp. Do not use custom fixtures or setups without permission from lab staff. Do not hold the material with your hands.
  6. Adjust the worktable to the appropriate height and lock it securely.
  7. Check that the tool can spin freely and is clear of the part.
  8. Consult the chart to determine the proper feed and speed for the hole and material. Adjust the machine to the appropriate speed.
  9. Remove extra tools and parts from the drill press. Check again that everything is clear of rotating and moving parts.
  10. Apply cutting lubricant to the part where appropriate for the material.

docs.title: Drilling
docs.text:
1. Turn on the machine. Do not leave it running unattended.
  2. Use peck drilling to remove material in 0.05-inch increments.
  3. Remove chips and swarf with a brush. Do not use a rag or your bare hands to remove chips.
  4. Apply additional cutting fluid as necessary throughout the operation.
  5. Reduce pressure when breaking through to prevent damage to the tool and part. Use a backing board to prevent the part from blowing out.
  6. Turn off the machine when finished. Do not attempt to slow it by hand.

docs.title: After Drilling
docs.text:
1. Carefully remove the part and tool from the machine. They may be hot; check before grabbing them.
  2. Use a brush and/or rag to clean chips, shavings, and oil from the drill press and surrounding area.
  3. Return all tools to their proper locations, power down the drill press, and tidy the work area.

docs.title: Good Drilling Practices
docs.text:
• Work from a drawing and project plan.
  • Lay out the workpiece properly before beginning.
  • Use additional light to illuminate the workpiece.
  • Step up to larger drill sizes. The diameter of the smaller drill bit should be no thicker than the web (distance between flutes) of the larger drill bit.
  • Support the tool with one hand when removing it from the chuck so it does not fall.

docs.title: Haas checklist
docs.text:
1. Put tools in tool holders
  2. Set tool offsets using tool probe
  3. Set fixture offset(s) with touch probe (usually G54)
  4. Load program
  5. Check that tool numbers in program match tools in machine
  6. Check that appropriate fixture offset is loaded
  7. Load stock in the machine
  8. Proof the part - test the program with air cuts. One easy way to do this is to add a height to the G54 Z value sufficient to make sure that all cuts will be above the top of the part surface.
  9. Use rapid and feed override at the beginning of the program to make sure that the initial Z axis moves are safe
  10. You can also use single block mode
  11. Keep your hand close to the emergency stop in case the program doesn't do what you expect
  12. Reset G54 to the correct value
  13. Run the program for the first time - follow the precautions in step 8 to make sure that nothing unexpected happens. You can adjust the feed rate override as needed.

docs.title: Vapor Silanization Rig Safe Operating Procedures
Location
docs.text: The vapor silanization rig is located in the first fume hood on your left when entering the microfluidics lab in Elings 3430.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Trimethylchlorosilane is flammable, toxic, and reacts with water vapor. It can make you sick if inhaled and ignite if it reacts with air or water vapor.
  • Use trimethylchlorosilane only in the vapor silanization rig inside a fume hood.
  • Do not let the pressure inside the chamber exceed 15 in Hg.
  • The silane valve must always be opened in a nitrogen atmosphere.
  • Wear protective eyewear, a lab coat, and gloves.
  • Keep the fume hood closed when you are not working inside it.
  • Consult the Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) before handling the silane.

The new glass reservoir has approximately 14 times the free liquid surface area of the previous reservoir. TMCS evaporates roughly 14 times faster than before! It will reach atmospheric pressure and leak within 2 hours if the silane valve is left open.

Open the silane valve only for the first 5 minutes of deposition. Then fully close the valve and continue the deposition for the required duration.

docs.title: Trimethylchlorosilane
docs.text:
Synonyms:

  • TMCS
  • Trimethylchlorosilane
  • Trimethylsilyl chloride

Formula: C₃H₉ClSi Molecular Weight: 108.64 g/mol CAS Number: 75-77-4 EC Number: 200-900-5

This protocol is intended for gas-phase monolayer deposition of a silane to serve as a counter-adhesion agent for glass or silicon substrates. Trimethylchlorosilane is referred to as “silane” throughout this protocol. It can be deposited onto silicon and glass substrates and can etch metal oxides, such as alumina.

docs.title: Operating Guidelines
docs.text:
1. Add yourself to the Silane Vapor Deposition Rig Log.

  1. Place your wafer inside the chamber. Check the O-ring seal. If dirty, wipe it with a Kimwipe. Ensure that the O-ring is fully seated in the groove.

  2. Pull a vacuum by turning on the pump and then opening the red “Vacuum” valve. When the pressure reads approximately 15 in Hg, turn the pump off and close the valve. Test the vacuum by waiting a minute or two and verifying that the pressure reading remains steady.

  3. Turn on the N₂ supply on the side of the fume hood. Turn the knob only once or twice.

  4. Open the silane chamber N₂ valve until the pressure reads approximately 5 in Hg. Then turn on the pump and open the vacuum valve until the pressure reads 15 in Hg. Repeat this cycle 5 times. Turn off the pump when finished.

  5. Turn the silane flask valve counterclockwise one full turn; the green masking tape should be on top. The pressure should begin to slowly drop. Wait approximately 5 minutes, then close the silane flask valve. There is now plenty of vapor in the chamber.

  1. Flip the sign to IN USE.

  2. Close the fume hood and set a timer for 40 minutes.

  3. When your cycle is complete, update the logbook with your end time.

  4. Open the N₂ valve until the pressure reads 5 in Hg. Open the vacuum valve until the pressure reads 15 in Hg. Repeat 5 times to purge the chamber again.

  5. Close the N₂ valve on the side of the fume hood.

  6. Remove your wafer.

  7. Flip the sign back to AVAILABLE and close the hood.

docs.title: Safety Considerations
docs.text:
• Always wear safety glasses when using the machine.
  • Always work with the machine cover closed.
  • NEVER leave the waterjet alone when running a job.
  • The machine door must be left open while you are away.
  • Ensure that the abrasive tanks are full.
  • Remove leftovers of used abrasive in the used abrasive bucket before running a new job.
  • Confirm that there are no leaks when running a job.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text:
Always check materials list BEFORE attempting to cut/engrave a material. If unsure contact IW Staff.

Allowed Materials:

  • Thin sheets of metal
  • Glass and ceramics (will produce larger kerfs)
  • Plastic (poor finish and will clog filters)
  • Rubber (poor finish and will clog filters)
  • Composites (will delaminate)

docs.title: Cutting with the Wazer Waterjet
docs.text:
Operating WAM to create a toolpath:

  • Open WAM (Wazercam software).
  • Import your DXF or SVG file into the software.

  • Scale and position your parts:

    • Importing the file may result in a change in dimensions, so double check the measurements are accurate before proceeding.
    • The grid in the software matches the plastic cut bed in the Wazer. Move your part(s) so that they will fit within your material and correspond to where you wish to cut.

  • Select Material

    • User Materials Tab: Scroll through the options and choose the material you are cutting and the corresponding thickness.
    • Wazer Materials Tab: If you are unable to find your allowed material in the "User Materials" tab, the material can also be chosen through the Wazer Materials tab, information on the type and thickness will need to be inputted manually.
    • If you do not see the material you are cutting, please contact a Wizard.

  • Select the cutting path offset. This will allow you to control how the kerf will affect your cut.

    • Outside: The tool will cut entirely outside of the file's boundary lines. Best when cutting the perimeter of a part.
    • Centerline: Tool cuts on top of the file's boundary lines. Best when cutting slots.
    • Inside: The tool will cut entirely inside of the file's boundary lines. Best when cutting out internal holes or parts where the scrap material will be located on the inside of the cut.

  • Select your tabs and leads. This will improve accuracy and prevent vibration/pop-ups, which can jam the waterjet and ruin the cut.

    • Usually 2-4 tabs is enough for most materials and thicknesses. For more complex cut geometries, the number of tabs should be increased.
    • Tab thickness should be proportional to material thickness, a good rule of thumb is for your tab thickness to be 30-50% of your material thickness. For very thin materials, we recommend a minimum tab thickness of 0.05“.
    • Tab locations may leave sharp edges along the cut. Avoid placing tabs in areas where dimensional accuracy is critical.
    • Disable leads unless your material is prone to delamination when cutting.

  • Select the cut quality. This will determine time for each job and the amount of abrasive used.

    • Fine typically provides the best results, although the differences in overall cut quality between settings are generally minimal.

  • Name your file and select "Generate Job File". Upload to the SD card located plugged into either the Waterjet or desktop computer. Eject SD card and plug into Waterjet.

Operating the Waterjet

  • Power on waterjet
    • Three switches (hidden switch to flip too) ...... add More detail
  • Select file using the arrow keys, follow prompted instructions and set up the tool. Ensure that a dry run is done before cutting and then close the hood and cut!

docs.title: Keyence 3D Image to STL
docs.text:
Important: 3D data must be collected using "Depth Up" on the Keyence microscope.

Keyence Software for Conversion

The Keyence microscope can use its motorized objective and focus sensing to create 3D depth maps by scanning the focal point of the microscope up and down across the sample.

This 3D data is saved within the .jpg or .tiff file and must be exported to a .csv file before converting it to an STL.

docs.title: Exporting .csv Data from .jpg or .tiff
docs.text:
Obtaining 3D data from these files requires the Keyence software. This software is available on the computer used for the CNC mill.

To find the software:

  1. Open the Windows Search bar.
  2. Search for vhx3d.
  3. Open the Keyence software.

Once the software is open, it will prompt you to select a file containing 3D data.

  1. Select the .jpg or .tiff file containing the 3D data.
  2. Select Save CSV.
  3. Choose where you want to save the .csv file.

The exported .csv file contains height data in microns (µm).

No X or Y data is provided in the CSV file. For the X and Y dimensions, refer to the Keyence microscope datasheet for the corresponding 3D pixel size.

docs.title: Converting the CSV Data to STL
docs.text: The CSV data can be converted into an STL mesh using MATLAB.

docs.title: 1. Download the MATLAB Scripts
docs.text:
Download the following MATLAB scripts:

  • surf2stl.m
  • stl_maker.m

Make sure both scripts are located in the same folder as the exported .csv file.

docs.title: 2. Open MATLAB
docs.text: Launch MATLAB and open the stl_maker.m script.

docs.title: 3. Set the CSV File Path
docs.text: Change the file path inside stl_maker.m so that it points to the exported .csv file.

docs.title: 4. Run the Script
docs.text:
Run stl_maker.m.

MATLAB will automatically generate the STL file and save it to:

This PC → Documents → MATLAB

The generated STL will use the CSV filename with _STL appended to it.

For example:

sample.csv

will generate:

sample_STL.stl

docs.title: 5. Import the STL
docs.text:
The exported STL is a mesh file representing the surface scan generated by the Keyence microscope.

The STL can be imported into SolidWorks or another mesh-editing program. From there, additional surfaces can be created and the mesh can be closed if a solid model is needed for 3D printing.

docs.title: Workflow Summary
docs.text:
Keyence Microscope
       ↓
Capture 3D Data using "Depth Up"
       ↓
Save as .JPG or .TIFF
       ↓
Open with Keyence VHX3D Software
       ↓
Save CSV
       ↓
CSV Height Data
       ↓
MATLAB (stl_maker.m + surf2stl.m)
       ↓
STL Mesh
       ↓
SolidWorks / Mesh Editor
       ↓
Closed Solid / 3D Printable Model

docs.title: Required Files
docs.text:
File Purpose .jpg / .tiff Keyence image containing embedded 3D data .csv Height data exported from Keyence software stl_maker.m MATLAB script used to generate the STL surf2stl.m MATLAB function used by stl_maker.m .stl Final surface mesh 
### GitHub folder structure

If this is going into your UCSB workshop GitHub repository, I'd organize the files like this:

```text
keyencemicroscope/
├── README.md
├── images/
│   ├── findsoftware.jpg
│   ├── exporting_data.jpg
│   └── urfilename.jpg
└── matlab/
    ├── stl_maker.m
    └── surf2stl.m

If you use that structure, change the image links in the README to:

![Finding the Keyence software](images/findsoftware.jpg)

![Exporting CSV data](images/exporting_data.jpg)

![Changing the CSV file path](images/urfilename.jpg)

And I'd recommend putting the MATLAB scripts directly in the repository rather than only telling users to download them separately, if you're allowed to distribute those scripts.

docs.title: Typical Use Cases
docs.text:
The Form 3 printers are liquid resin stereolithographic 3D printers capable of producing high resolution accurate models out of a variety of materials. Liquid resin printers use a bath of reactive resin which is precisely cured using specific wavelengths of light. This printer is particularly well suited for thin, high aspect ratio features and models requiring great surface accuracy.

Based on the material and application, some prints will benefit from post process UV curing to strengthen and harden the finished part. See part curing documentation in UV FormCure reference documentation.

The Form 3 is generally used when the Bambu FDM printers cannot meet the required surface finish, material properties, or feature size. They are extremely versatile, with resins that are clear, tough, rigid, flexible, ESD-safe, and more.

Depending on the resin you use, the Form 3 printers are great for: - Microfluidic PDMS Molds - Vacuum chamber fixturing - Light-duty tooling, such as custom wrench sockets - Low volume injection molds - Autoclavable devices - Flexible devices - High-aspect ratio and thin-walled devices, where FDM printing would struggle

docs.title: Key Differences Between the Form 3 and Form 4
docs.text: The Form 4 offers a significant decrease in print speed compared to the Form 3. While the Form 3 uses a laser-based printing process, the Form 4 uses Low Force Display (LFD) technology, allowing it to cure an entire layer at once. This greatly reduces print times, especially for larger parts or batches of multiple parts. As a result, the Form 4 can produce parts much faster while maintaining the high level of detail and surface quality expected from Formlabs SLA printers.

docs.text: Tool Type: CO2 Laser cutter and engraver Manufacturer: ThunderLaser USA Location: Elings 3430

docs.title: Safety Concerns
docs.text:
This machine uses a class 4 carbon dioxide (CO2) laser that emits intense and invisible laser radiation. The direct radiation or even diffuse reflected radiation is dangerous!

  • NEVER leave the laser machine alone when running a job. If you do need to leave, make sure there is someone else nearby who is aware that it is on and cutting.
  • The machine door must be left open while you are away if no one is nearby to keep watch.
  • Do not store any flammable materials on the inside of the device or in the immediate vicinity of the device.
  • If left behind, remove leftover materials before running a job.
  • A fire extinguisher and fire blanket are on the right of the device as the laser beam can ignite flammable materials.
  • Metals, particularly copper, silver, gold and un-coated aluminum, cannot be processed with the laser as they causes high reflections of the laser beam.
  • Before processing materials the user must verify whether harmful materials can be produced and whether the filter equipment of the exhaust system is suitable for the harmful materials.
  • PVC (polyvinyl chloride) must under no circumstances be processed with the laser.
  • Looking directly into the laser can cause retinal damage.
  • Ensure that the air-assist is working properly before firing the laser. If the air assist is malfunctioning, the laser cannot be safely operated.
  • Confirm that the fume collection system is running whenever the laser is cutting or engraving.

docs.title: Harrick Plasma Chamber PDC-32G
docs.text: Tool Type: Surface treatment Location: Elings 3430 Description: Plasma chamber Manufacturer: Harrick

docs.title: About
docs.text:
The Harrick PDC-32G is a compact tabletop plasma cleaner for nanoscale surface cleaning and activation of small samples. The attached PlasmaFlo gas mixer allows quantitative control of up to two different process gases and monitoring of the vacuum pressure within the chamber.

This tool is plumbed for nitrogen plasma only, which works well for PDMS-to-glass and PDMS-to-PDMS bonding. If you require oxygen plasma, consider using the plasma chamber in the Nanostructures Cleanroom Facility.

docs.title: Safety Concerns
docs.text:
• The plasma chamber uses RF radiation.
  • If you have a pacemaker or similar device, consult your doctor before using this tool.

docs.title: Training Documentation
docs.text: • Plasma Cleaner SOP

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text:
Brian Dincau found that the following recipe works well for bonding PDMS to PDMS or glass:

  • Power: High
  • Pressure: 440–460 mTorr
  • Duration: 30 seconds
  • Nitrogen Flow: Adjust as needed to maintain the desired pressure.
  • After Treatment: Mate the surfaces immediately, then transfer to an oven at 115°C for 20 minutes.

docs.title: Vapor Silanization Chamber
docs.text: Tool Type: Surface treatment Location: Elings 3430 Description: Vacuum deposition chamber Manufacturer: Fisher Scientific

docs.title: About
docs.text: The vapor silanization rig is located in the first fume hood on your left when entering the microfluidics lab in Elings 3430.

docs.title: Safety Concerns
docs.text:
• Trimethylchlorosilane is flammable, toxic, and reacts with water vapor. It can cause illness if inhaled and may ignite when reacting with air or water vapor.
  • Use trimethylchlorosilane only in the vapor silanization rig inside a fume hood.
  • Do not let the pressure inside the chamber exceed 15 in Hg.
  • Open the silane valve only in a nitrogen atmosphere.
  • Wear protective eyewear, a lab coat, and gloves.
  • Keep the fume hood closed when you are not working inside it.
  • Consult the Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) before handling the silane.

docs.title: Training Documentation
docs.text: • Vapor Silanization Rig Safe Operating Procedures

docs.title: Trimethylchlorosilane
docs.text:
Synonyms:

  • TMCS
  • Trimethylchlorosilane
  • Trimethylsilyl chloride

Formula: C₃H₉ClSi Molecular Weight: 108.64 g/mol CAS Number: 75-77-4 EC Number: 200-900-5

This protocol is intended for gas-phase monolayer deposition of a silane to serve as a counter-adhesion agent for glass or silicon substrates. Trimethylchlorosilane is referred to as “silane” throughout the protocol. It can be deposited onto silicon and glass substrates and can etch metal oxides, such as alumina.
